section: One Import is All You Need
text:
One Import is All You Need

library(tidyverse)   # readr + dplyr + tidyr + ggplot2 + ...

Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.4.3



The tidyverse is a bundle of packages that share a design philosophy. Loading it gives us readr (loading), dplyr (transforming) and tidyr (reshaping) all at once.


Point out the startup message: it lists the attached packages and flags any conflicts (e.g. dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()). This is normal. Contrast with library(dplyr) alone from last week — today we want the whole toolkit.

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
Reading a CSV






ImportantTask



Load data/penguins.csv and take a look. What type of object comes back?




penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv")
penguins

# A tibble: 344 × 9
   rowid species island    bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm
   <dbl> <chr>   <chr>              <dbl>         <dbl>             <dbl>
 1     1 Adelie  Torgersen           39.1          18.7               181
 2     2 Adelie  Torgersen           39.5          17.4               186
 3     3 Adelie  Torgersen           40.3          18                 195
 4     4 Adelie  Torgersen           NA            NA                  NA
 5     5 Adelie  Torgersen           36.7          19.3               193
 6     6 Adelie  Torgersen           39.3          20.6               190
 7     7 Adelie  Torgersen           38.9          17.8               181
 8     8 Adelie  Torgersen           39.2          19.6               195
 9     9 Adelie  Torgersen           34.1          18.1               193
10    10 Adelie  Torgersen           42            20.2               190
# ℹ 334 more rows
# ℹ 3 more variables: body_mass_g <dbl>, sex <chr>, year <dbl>




CSV = Comma Separated Values: plain text, columns split by ,, rows split by a newline. read_csv() returns a tibble — a modern data frame with nicer printing.


Open penguins.csv in a text editor first so they see the commas and the header row. Note the column-type spec read_csv prints — it guessed <dbl>, <chr> etc. for us. Emphasise: the printout tells you the dimensions and the type of every column.

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
Other delimiters






ImportantTask



The file data/penguins_pipe.txt holds the same data, but columns are separated by | instead of ,. Try read_csv() on it — then load it properly.




read_delim("data/penguins_pipe.txt", delim = "|")

# A tibble: 344 × 9
   rowid species island    bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm
   <dbl> <chr>   <chr>              <dbl>         <dbl>             <dbl>
 1     1 Adelie  Torgersen           39.1          18.7               181
 2     2 Adelie  Torgersen           39.5          17.4               186
 3     3 Adelie  Torgersen           40.3          18                 195
 4     4 Adelie  Torgersen           NA            NA                  NA
 5     5 Adelie  Torgersen           36.7          19.3               193
 6     6 Adelie  Torgersen           39.3          20.6               190
 7     7 Adelie  Torgersen           38.9          17.8               181
 8     8 Adelie  Torgersen           39.2          19.6               195
 9     9 Adelie  Torgersen           34.1          18.1               193
10    10 Adelie  Torgersen           42            20.2               190
# ℹ 334 more rows
# ℹ 3 more variables: body_mass_g <dbl>, sex <chr>, year <dbl>




read_csv() is just read_delim() with delim = ",". For any other delimiter (tabs → read_tsv(), or anything via read_delim(delim = ...)) you pick the matching reader.


First do read_csv("data/penguins_pipe.txt") and let it fail / mangle — everything lands in one column. The lesson: look at the file (open it) to find the delimiter, then choose the reader. Mention that if you don’t know the format you experiment until it loads.

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
The five verbs
dplyr gives us a small set of readable verbs:


mutate() — add or change columns
select() — pick columns
filter() — pick rows
arrange() — reorder rows
summarise() — collapse many rows to a summary




We’ll demo them on gapminder: country-level life expectancy, population and GDP per capita over time.



library(gapminder)
gapminder

# A tibble: 1,704 × 6
   country     continent  year lifeExp      pop gdpPercap
   <fct>       <fct>     <int>   <dbl>    <int>     <dbl>
 1 Afghanistan Asia       1952    28.8  8425333      779.
 2 Afghanistan Asia       1957    30.3  9240934      821.
 3 Afghanistan Asia       1962    32.0 10267083      853.
 4 Afghanistan Asia       1967    34.0 11537966      836.
 5 Afghanistan Asia       1972    36.1 13079460      740.
 6 Afghanistan Asia       1977    38.4 14880372      786.
 7 Afghanistan Asia       1982    39.9 12881816      978.
 8 Afghanistan Asia       1987    40.8 13867957      852.
 9 Afghanistan Asia       1992    41.7 16317921      649.
10 Afghanistan Asia       1997    41.8 22227415      635.
# ℹ 1,694 more rows




glimpse(gapminder) is a nice alternative view — shows every column down the page. Point out it is a tall dataset: one row per country per year. We’ll come back to that word “tall” for tidyr.

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
mutate: add a column






ImportantTask



Add a column gdp_billions = GDP per capita × population ÷ 1e9.




gapminder |>
  mutate(gdp_billions = gdpPercap * pop / 1e9)

# A tibble: 1,704 × 7
   country     continent  year lifeExp      pop gdpPercap gdp_billions
   <fct>       <fct>     <int>   <dbl>    <int>     <dbl>        <dbl>
 1 Afghanistan Asia       1952    28.8  8425333      779.         6.57
 2 Afghanistan Asia       1957    30.3  9240934      821.         7.59
 3 Afghanistan Asia       1962    32.0 10267083      853.         8.76
 4 Afghanistan Asia       1967    34.0 11537966      836.         9.65
 5 Afghanistan Asia       1972    36.1 13079460      740.         9.68
 6 Afghanistan Asia       1977    38.4 14880372      786.        11.7 
 7 Afghanistan Asia       1982    39.9 12881816      978.        12.6 
 8 Afghanistan Asia       1987    40.8 13867957      852.        11.8 
 9 Afghanistan Asia       1992    41.7 16317921      649.        10.6 
10 Afghanistan Asia       1997    41.8 22227415      635.        14.1 
# ℹ 1,694 more rows




The pipe |> feeds gapminder into mutate() as its first argument. Read it as “take gapminder, then mutate”.

title: Data Wrangling in R
section: Tidyverse functions don’t modify their input
text:
Tidyverse functions don’t modify their input






ImportantTask



Check: does gapminder now have a gdp_billions column?




gapminder$gdp_billions

Warning: Unknown or uninitialised column: `gdp_billions`.


NULL




NULL (or an error) — mutate() returned a copy; it never touched the original. To keep the change we must assign it back.



gapminder <- gapminder |>
  mutate(gdp_billions = gdpPercap * pop / 1e9)



Tidyverse verbs are pure functions — input in, new tibble out, original untouched. More in the functional programming chapter.

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
filter: pick rows






ImportantTask



Keep only the rows for Asia, then show country, year, gdp_billions.




gapminder |>
  filter(continent == "Asia") |>
  select(country, year, gdp_billions)

# A tibble: 396 × 3
   country      year gdp_billions
   <fct>       <int>        <dbl>
 1 Afghanistan  1952         6.57
 2 Afghanistan  1957         7.59
 3 Afghanistan  1962         8.76
 4 Afghanistan  1967         9.65
 5 Afghanistan  1972         9.68
 6 Afghanistan  1977        11.7 
 7 Afghanistan  1982        12.6 
 8 Afghanistan  1987        11.8 
 9 Afghanistan  1992        10.6 
10 Afghanistan  1997        14.1 
# ℹ 386 more rows




Note the double ==: filter() keeps rows where the condition is TRUE.


Live pitfall to demo: put the select() before the filter() and filter on a column you dropped — you get an error, because by then the continent column is gone. Great illustration that the pipe is a sequence: each step only sees the output of the one before it.

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
arrange: reorder rows






ImportantTask



Order the Asian countries from highest gdp_billions to lowest.




gapminder |>
  filter(continent == "Asia") |>
  select(country, year, gdp_billions) |>
  arrange(desc(gdp_billions))

# A tibble: 396 × 3
   country  year gdp_billions
   <fct>   <int>        <dbl>
 1 China    2007        6540.
 2 Japan    2007        4035.
 3 China    2002        3994.
 4 Japan    2002        3635.
 5 Japan    1997        3630.
 6 Japan    1992        3335.
 7 China    1997        2816.
 8 Japan    1987        2732.
 9 India    2007        2723.
10 Japan    1982        2296.
# ℹ 386 more rows




arrange() sorts ascending by default; wrap a column in desc() for descending.

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
summarise: many rows → one






ImportantTask



What is the mean gdp_billions across all Asian rows?




gapminder |>
  filter(continent == "Asia") |>
  summarise(mean_gdp = mean(gdp_billions))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_gdp
     <dbl>
1     227.




summarise() collapses a whole tibble to a single row. It works with mean, median, sum, min, max, and counts via n() / n_distinct().


This feels underwhelming on its own — one number. The payoff is the next slide: summarise() becomes powerful once we tell it to work per group.

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
group_by + summarise






ImportantTask



Compute the mean life expectancy for each continent.




gapminder |>
  group_by(continent) |>
  summarise(avg_lifeExp = mean(lifeExp))

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  continent avg_lifeExp
  <fct>           <dbl>
1 Africa           48.9
2 Americas         64.7
3 Asia             60.1
4 Europe           71.9
5 Oceania          74.3




group_by() doesn’t change the data — it tags it. The next summarise() then runs once per group, giving one row per continent.


Do gapminder |> group_by(continent) on its own first: the printout gains a Groups: continent [5] line but the rows look identical. Then add the summarise and watch it collapse. That “tag, then aggregate” model is the thing to land.

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
A real question






ImportantTask



Which countries have the highest average GDP since 1960?



We first need to parse this into a sequence of verbs:

Group by country,
Filter to years after 1960,
Summarize to get the average GDP (bonus: max, and number of records).




gapminder |>
  filter(year > 1960) |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(
    mean_gdp = mean(gdp_billions),
    max_gdp  = max(gdp_billions),
    n_years  = n(),
    .groups  = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_gdp))

# A tibble: 142 × 4
   country        mean_gdp max_gdp n_years
   <fct>             <dbl>   <dbl>   <int>
 1 United States     7200.  12934.      10
 2 Japan             2476.   4035.      10
 3 China             1981.   6540.      10
 4 Germany           1828.   2651.      10
 5 United Kingdom    1221.   2018.      10
 6 France            1181.   1861.      10
 7 Italy             1039.   1661.      10
 8 India              990.   2723.      10
 9 Brazil             945.   1723.      10
10 Mexico             689.   1302.      10
# ℹ 132 more rows




This is the centrepiece — build it line by line, re-running after each pipe so they see the tibble grow columns. Points to make live:

n() counts rows in each group.
.groups = "drop" silences the “grouped output” message (optional, but tidy).
If mean/max ever return NA, add na.rm = TRUE — demo by introducing an NA if you have time.

text:
Shortcut: count






ImportantTask



How many countries are in each continent in 2007?




gapminder |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  count(continent)

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  continent     n
  <fct>     <int>
1 Africa       52
2 Americas     25
3 Asia         33
4 Europe       30
5 Oceania       2




count(continent) is just a tidy shorthand for group_by(continent) |> summarise(n = n()).

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
Long vs. wide
gapminder is tall — many rows per country. Sometimes we want years as columns instead, e.g. to compare 1952 with 2007 directly.






ImportantTask



Reshape so each row is a country and each year is its own lifeExp column.




gapminder_wide <- gapminder |>
  select(country, year, lifeExp) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = lifeExp)
gapminder_wide

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
Using the wide shape






ImportantTask



Compute the change in life expectancy from 1952 to 2007 for each country.




gapminder_wide |>
  mutate(change = `2007` - `1952`) |>
  select(country, change)

# A tibble: 142 × 2
   country     change
   <fct>        <dbl>
 1 Afghanistan   15.0
 2 Albania       21.2
 3 Algeria       29.2
 4 Angola        12.7
 5 Argentina     12.8
 6 Australia     12.1
 7 Austria       13.0
 8 Bahrain       24.7
 9 Bangladesh    26.6
10 Belgium       11.4
# ℹ 132 more rows




The backticks around `2007` and `1952` tell R these are column names, not numbers. You’d need them for any name with spaces or symbols too.

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
The inverse: pivot_longer






ImportantTask



Turn the wide table back into a tall one.




gapminder_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -country,
    names_to = "year",
    values_to = "lifeExp"
  )

# A tibble: 1,704 × 3
   country     year  lifeExp
   <fct>       <chr>   <dbl>
 1 Afghanistan 1952     28.8
 2 Afghanistan 1957     30.3
 3 Afghanistan 1962     32.0
 4 Afghanistan 1967     34.0
 5 Afghanistan 1972     36.1
 6 Afghanistan 1977     38.4
 7 Afghanistan 1982     39.9
 8 Afghanistan 1987     40.8
 9 Afghanistan 1992     41.7
10 Afghanistan 1997     41.8
# ℹ 1,694 more rows




cols = -country means “every column except country” — a tidyselect helper, so we don’t list all the years by hand.


pivot_longer and pivot_wider are inverses. Note year comes back as <chr> text, not a number — it was a column name a moment ago. A quick mutate(year = as.integer(year)) fixes it if asked. Also mention separate_wider_delim() from the notes for splitting one column into two (the table3 “cases/population” case) if time allows.

First do read_csv("data/penguins_pipe.txt") and let it fail / mangle — everything lands in one column. The lesson: look at the file (open it) to find the delimiter, then choose the reader. Mention that if you don’t know the format you experiment until it loads.

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
The five verbs
dplyr gives us a small set of readable verbs:


mutate() — add or change columns
select() — pick columns
filter() — pick rows
arrange() — reorder rows
summarise() — collapse many rows to a summary

Tidyverse functions don’t modify their input






Task


Check: does gapminder now have a gdp_billions column?





gapminder$gdp_billions

NULL

gapminder <- gapminder |>

Task

gapminder |>

arrange: reorder rows






Task


Order the Asian countries from highest gdp_billions to lowest.





gapminder |>
  filter(continent == "Asia") |>
  select(country, year, gdp_billions) |>
  arrange(desc(gdp_billions))

# A tibble: 396 × 3
   country  year gdp_billions
   <fct>   <int>        <dbl>
 1 China    2007        6540.
 2 Japan    2007        4035.

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
summarise: many rows → one






Task


What is the mean gdp_billions across all Asian rows?





gapminder |>
  filter(continent == "Asia") |>
  summarise(mean_gdp = mean(gdp_billions))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_gdp
     <dbl>
1     227.




summarise() collapses a whole tibble to a single row. It works with mean, median, sum, min, max, and counts via n() / n_distinct().


This feels underwhelming on its own — one number. The payoff is the next slide: summarise() becomes powerful once we tell it to work per group.

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
group_by + summarise






Task


Compute the mean life expectancy for each continent.





gapminder |>
  group_by(continent) |>
  summarise(avg_lifeExp = mean(lifeExp))

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  continent avg_lifeExp
  <fct>           <dbl>
1 Africa           48.9
2 Americas         64.7
3 Asia             60.1
4 Europe           71.9
5 Oceania          74.3




group_by() doesn’t change the data — it tags it. The next summarise() then runs once per group, giving one row per continent.


Do gapminder |> group_by(continent) on its own first: the printout gains a Groups: continent [5] line but the rows look identical. Then add the summarise and watch it collapse. That “tag, then aggregate” model is the thing to land.

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
A real question






Task


Which countries have the highest average GDP since 1960?




We first need to parse this into a sequence of verbs:

Group by country,
Filter to years after 1960,
Summarize to get the average GDP (bonus: max, and number of records).




gapminder |>
  filter(year > 1960) |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(
    mean_gdp = mean(gdp_billions),
    max_gdp  = max(gdp_billions),
    n_years  = n(),
    .groups  = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_gdp))

# A tibble: 142 × 4
   country        mean_gdp max_gdp n_years
   <fct>             <dbl>   <dbl>   <int>
 1 United States     7200.  12934.      10
 2 Japan             2476.   4035.      10
 3 China             1981.   6540.      10
 4 Germany           1828.   2651.      10
 5 United Kingdom    1221.   2018.      10
 6 France            1181.   1861.      10
 7 Italy             1039.   1661.      10
 8 India              990.   2723.      10
 9 Brazil             945.   1723.      10
10 Mexico             689.   1302.      10
# ℹ 132 more rows

n() counts rows in each group.
.groups = "drop" silences the “grouped output” message (optional, but tidy).
If mean/max ever return NA, add na.rm = TRUE — demo by introducing an NA if you have time.

The inverse: pivot_longer






Task

gapminder_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -country,
    names_to = "year",
    values_to = "lifeExp"

# A tibble: 1,704 × 3

title: Coding in R
text:
Your first variables






ImportantTask



Create three variables — a number, some text, and a truth value — then ask R what type each one is.




x <- 5
y <- "Hello"
z <- TRUE

typeof(x)

[1] "double"

typeof(y)

[1] "character"

typeof(z)

[1] "logical"




Point out double, character, logical. Mention the chapter’s aside: <- is idiomatic R, = is fine, both accepted in assessments.

title: Coding in R
text:
R is dynamically typed






ImportantTask



Demonstrate dynamic typing in R




number <- 5
typeof(number)

[1] "double"

number <- "hello"
typeof(number)

[1] "character"




R does not require variable types. It also does not check types when you call a function!

title: Coding in R
text:
Building vectors






ImportantTask



Make a vector of the numbers 1 to 5 with c(), then check its type and length. What happens if you check the length of the plain number x from before?




vector <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

typeof(vector)   # still "double"!

[1] "double"

length(vector)

[1] 5

length(x)        # scalars ARE length-1 vectors

[1] 1




In R there are no scalars — everything is a vector.

title: Coding in R
text:
Indexing: R counts from 1






ImportantTask



Get the 2nd element, the 5th element, and elements 2 through 4.




vector[2]

[1] 2

vector[5]     # the LAST element — it would be index 4 in Python!

[1] 5

vector[2:4]

[1] 2 3 4




Show vector[0]: it returns an empty vector, no error.

title: Coding in R
text:
Logical indexing






ImportantTask



Use a vector of TRUE/FALSE to pick out elements — then negate it with ! to pick the others.




elements <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)

vector[elements]    # positions 1, 3, 4

[1] 1 3 4

vector[!elements]   # elementwise negation: positions 2, 5

[1] 2 5




This is the idiom that powers filtering data in every week to come.

title: Coding in R
text:
Lists: containers for anything






ImportantTask



Build a list about a penguin — two bits of text, a numeric vector, and a count — then pull out elements by name and by position.




l <- list(
  name = "Flipper",
  species = "Adelie",
  measurements = c(210, 217, 230),
  n_measurements = 3
)

l$name

[1] "Flipper"

l$measurements

[1] 210 217 230

l[[3]]

[1] 210 217 230




Demo the difference between [3] and [[3]] - a list vs. the element. Comment on why the names might be better than the numbers.

Data frames: lists of equal-length vectors






ImportantTask



Build a small table of penguins — name, species, flipper length — then get a column with $, a row with [2, ], and a single entry.




df <- data.frame(
  name              = c("Flipper", "Tux", "Pingu"),
  species           = c("Adelie", "Gentoo", "Emperor"),
  flipper_length_mm = c(210, 217, 230)
)

df

     name species flipper_length_mm
1 Flipper  Adelie               210
2     Tux  Gentoo               217
3   Pingu Emperor               230

df$name              # access a column

[1] "Flipper" "Tux"     "Pingu"  

df$flipper_length_mm

[1] 210 217 230

df[2, ]              # row 2

  name species flipper_length_mm
2  Tux  Gentoo               217

df[2, "species"]     # single entry

[1] "Gentoo"









TipTibbles

if_else: a vectorised conditional






ImportantTask



Classify each element of x <- c(3, 1, 4, 1, 5) as “big” or “small” depending on whether it exceeds 2.




library(dplyr)

Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.4.3



Attaching package: 'dplyr'


The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':

    filter, lag


The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

x <- c(3, 1, 4, 1, 5)

if_else(x > 2, "big", "small")

[1] "big"   "small" "big"   "small" "big"

title: Coding in R
text:
case_when: many conditions






ImportantTask



Classify x as “small” (< 2), “medium” (< 5), or “large” (everything else).




case_when(
  x < 2 ~ "small",
  x < 5 ~ "medium",
  TRUE  ~ "large"
)

[1] "medium" "small"  "medium" "small"  "large" 




Order matters: swap the first two conditions and “small” disappears.

title: Coding in R
text:
Writing Functions






ImportantTask



Write a function add(x, y).




add <- function(x, y) {
  x + y        # the LAST expression is the return value
}

add(1, 10)

[1] 11




No return() needed.

title: Coding in R
text:
Guard clauses: return






ImportantTask



Write clip(x, lower, upper) that forces a value into a range — e.g. for cleaning impossible measurements.




clip <- function(x, lower, upper) {
  if (x < lower) return(lower)   # guard clause
  if (x > upper) return(upper)
  x                              # still here? it's in range
}

clip(5, 0, 10)

[1] 5

clip(-3, 0, 10)

[1] 0

clip(42, 0, 10)

[1] 10




Note that you could also use case_when to do this

title: Coding in R
text:
Functions are Variables


sapply(1:10, function(x) clip(x, 3, 7))

 [1] 3 3 3 4 5 6 7 7 7 7




A function you never named — an anonymous function — passed straight into sapply.
It is called a “higher order function.”

title: Coding in R
text:
Composing functions: f(g(x))

times_ten <- function(y) y * 10
add_five <- function(x) x + 5

x <- 10
times_ten(add_five(x))


Readable — up to a point.

title: Coding in R
text:
The pipe: |>






ImportantTask



Implement the above logic using the pipe operator |>




x |> add_five() |> times_ten()

[1] 150




Much more readable.


The parentheses after each function are required — the pipe inserts the left-hand side into the FIRST argument.
Mention %>% (magrittr) exists and behaves almost identically, but |> is base R.

When you’re stuck

?mean — documentation (also ?dplyr, even ?`+`)
example(mean) — run the docs’ examples
??"linear regression" — search all installed packages
Read the error message first — then search it verbatim online







TipAI tools



Great for getting unblocked — but they hallucinate. Verify everything with ?, and never paste sensitive data into them. The docs are always right; the AI is usually helpful.

[1] 2

vector[5]     # the LAST element — it would be index 4 in Python!

[1] 5

vector[2:4]

[1] 2 3 4




Show vector[0]: it returns an empty vector, no error.

title: Coding in R
text:
Logical indexing






Task


Use a vector of TRUE/FALSE to pick out elements — then negate it with ! to pick the others.





elements <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)

vector[elements]    # positions 1, 3, 4

[1] 1 3 4

vector[!elements]   # elementwise negation: positions 2, 5

[1] 2 5




This is the idiom that powers filtering data in every week to come.

Task


Build a list about a penguin — two bits of text, a numeric vector, and a count — then pull out elements by name and by position.





l <- list(
  name = "Flipper",
  species = "Adelie",
  measurements = c(210, 217, 230),
  n_measurements = 3
)

l$name

[1] "Flipper"

l$measurements

[1] 210 217 230

l[[3]]

[1] 210 217 230




Demo the difference between [3] and [[3]] - a list vs. the element. Comment on why the names might be better than the numbers.

  name              = c("Flipper", "Tux", "Pingu"),
  species           = c("Adelie", "Gentoo", "Emperor"),
  flipper_length_mm = c(210, 217, 230)
)

df

1 Flipper  Adelie               210
2     Tux  Gentoo               217
3   Pingu Emperor               230

df$name              # access a column

[1] "Flipper" "Tux"     "Pingu"

[1] 210 217 230

2  Tux  Gentoo               217

text:
if_else: a vectorised conditional






Task


Classify each element of x <- c(3, 1, 4, 1, 5) as “big” or “small” depending on whether it exceeds 2.





library(dplyr)
x <- c(3, 1, 4, 1, 5)

if_else(x > 2, "big", "small")

[1] "big"   "small" "big"   "small" "big"

title: Coding in R
text:
case_when: many conditions






Task


Classify x as “small” (< 2), “medium” (< 5), or “large” (everything else).





case_when(
  x < 2 ~ "small",
  x < 5 ~ "medium",
  TRUE  ~ "large"
)

[1] "medium" "small"  "medium" "small"  "large" 




Order matters: swap the first two conditions and “small” disappears.

title: Coding in R
text:
Writing Functions






Task


Write a function add(x, y).





add <- function(x, y) {
  x + y        # the LAST expression is the return value
}

add(1, 10)

[1] 11




No return() needed.

title: Coding in R
text:
Guard clauses: return






Task


Write clip(x, lower, upper) that forces a value into a range — e.g. for cleaning impossible measurements.





clip <- function(x, lower, upper) {
  if (x < lower) return(lower)   # guard clause
  if (x > upper) return(upper)
  x                              # still here? it's in range
}

clip(5, 0, 10)

[1] 5

clip(-3, 0, 10)

[1] 0

clip(42, 0, 10)

[1] 10




Note that you could also use case_when to do this

title: Coding in R
text:
Functions are Variables


sapply(1:10, function(x) clip(x, 3, 7))

 [1] 3 3 3 4 5 6 7 7 7 7




A function you never named — an anonymous function — passed straight into sapply.
It is called a “higher order function.”

title: Coding in R
text:
Composing functions: f(g(x))

times_ten <- function(y) y * 10
add_five <- function(x) x + 5

x <- 10
times_ten(add_five(x))


Readable — up to a point.

title: Coding in R
text:
The pipe: |>






Task


Implement the above logic using the pipe operator |>





x |> add_five() |> times_ten()

[1] 150




Much more readable.


The parentheses after each function are required — the pipe inserts the left-hand side into the FIRST argument.
Mention %>% (magrittr) exists and behaves almost identically, but |> is base R.

title: Coding in R
text:
When you’re stuck

?mean — documentation (also ?dplyr, even ?`+`)
example(mean) — run the docs’ examples
??"linear regression" — search all installed packages
Read the error message first — then search it verbatim online







AI tools


Great for getting unblocked — but they hallucinate. Verify everything with ?, and never paste sensitive data into them. The docs are always right; the AI is usually helpful.
